extracted.intended_audience: architects, artists, art critics, and students of art and architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging and producing architecture, ornament, and painting: prioritizing technical soundness, visible technical mastery, appropriate ornament, and the evidence of honest manual labour as signs of value. Applicable to critics, practitioners, and students evaluating works of art and buildings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice with devotion and respect necessary to perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Very important whether [the arts] are practised with the devotion and regarded with the respect which are necessary or due to their perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The relative rank of arts is less important than whether an art is pursued with the devotion and respect required for its perfection; focus on how an art is practiced rather than quarrels over comparative dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value measured by balanced perfection and harmony among faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: The true perfection of any of [the human faculties] is not possible without some relative perfection of the others; the perfection of any single power is ... to be valued by the harmony which it indicates among the other powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate arts by how well bodily, moral, and intellectual faculties work together (examples: senses quicken feeling which quickens understanding and imagination; overdevelopment of one faculty can undermine others — e.g., morbid feeling weakening understanding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three stages of bodily dexterity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physical skill ... is manifested in three stages: First, Bodily power by practice; Secondly, Bodily power by moral habit; Thirdly, Bodily power by immediate energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the degree to which an art admits and requires each stage (e.g., a smith mainly requires practice; fencing/shooting/riding admit moral habit; fine arts admit expression of the whole man).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of arts by orders (bodily, intelligent, imaginative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The arts whose chief element is bodily dexterity are of the third order; the next step is arts of the second order (joined with intelligence not connected with bodily dexterity); the arts of the first order join the Imaginative part of the intellect and the Sensitive part of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate an art by which faculties it primarily engages: third-order (handicrafts, bodily skill), second-order (war, medicine — intelligence and stratagem), first-order (poetry, architecture, painting — imagination + feeling). Recognize overlap and that a great practitioner can elevate a 'lower' art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical mastery visible at a glance (instinctive judgments)
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought to be able to tell good painting by a side glance ... this mastery of the language is that of which we should be cognizant by a glance of the eye; and if that be not found, it is wasted time to look farther.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quick visual instinct to detect technical command of medium (color, line, execution). If a painter lacks technical language mastery, their moral or poetic feeling in paint is likely wasted; technical excellence is an index of deeper expressional worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical qualities are primary in architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Good building is necessary to good expression, comes before it, and is to be primarily looked for; the manner of building is capable of being determinately estimated and classed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging architecture, assess structural soundness, common-sense in structure, and technical composition first to discard absurdities (e.g., incongruous historical pastiches) before attempting to appraise expressive qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament must be inherent and necessary to the building
rubrics_metrics.description: A noble building never has any extraneous or superfluous ornament; all its parts are necessary to its loveliness, and that no single atom of them could be removed without harm to its life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between inherent architectural ornament (integral to design) and removable decoration (curtains, pictures, bracelets). Only ornament that is part of the building's inherent beauty counts as true architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good ornament well-placed is never overcharged; bad ornament is always overcharged
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament cannot be overcharged if it is good, and is always overcharged when it is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement matters: what is 'good' must be appropriate to its context (a gold ring is a good ornament on a finger, not on an under-lip). Objections about 'overcharging by misplacement' are equivalent to saying an ornament is bad; good ornament, properly placed, is not excessive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of manual labour as a chief source of value in ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: The appearance of labor, that is to say, the evidence of the past industry of man, is always, in the abstract, intensely delightful ... the utter absence of it destroys good in human work. Machine ornaments are no ornaments at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value visible signs of honest, skilled manual work in ornamentation; they register human industry and authenticity. Machine-produced or ornament that shows no labour is devalued; the presence of hand-labour signals value and delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour may be negative when it substitutes for thought or skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever labour replaces what was better than labour, that is to say, skill and thought; wherever it substitutes itself for these ... then it is positive evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish useful evidence of labour from labour that indicates weakness, folly, or wasted effort (examples: excessive labour doing what could be done by thought or skill). Signs of toil that reveal incompetence or misdirected effort detract from value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical and expressional correspondence differs between painting and architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a correspondence between the technical and expressional parts of architecture; not a true or entire correspondence, so that when the expression is best, the building must be also best; but so much of correspondence as that good building is necessary to good expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that in painting technical execution and expression are more tightly linked (execution often equals expression); in architecture, technical assessment is more determinable and should be used to limit works for later expressive appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist's mastery of medium determines expressive worth
rubrics_metrics.description: If the man be a painter indeed, and have the gift of colors and lines, what is in him will come from his hand freely and faithfully; and the language itself is so difficult and so vast, that the mere possession of it argues the man is great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give high value to artists who demonstrably master their technical language (color, line, handling). Technical command enables faithful conveyance of feeling and subject; lack of technical ability in a would-be artist means their moral/poetical content is misapplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical considerations (sightlines, acoustics, material suitability) affect architectural beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: A stone pillar, even when solid, must be quite as thick as is either graceful or convenient, and in modern churches is often too thick as it is, hindering sight of the preacher, and checking the sound of his voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating architectural elements (e.g., column form/shaft strength), weigh engineering/material realities and human use — avoid forms that, though theoretically interesting, impair function (visibility, acoustics, space).
